# Elon Musk says Tesla will use Intel 14A technology at its $20bn TeraFab project in Austin

World’s richest man also detailed how production at the fab will be divided between Tesla and SpaceX

April 23, 2026By[Charlotte Trueman](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/profile/Charlotte-Trueman/)[Have your say](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/elon-musk-says-tesla-will-use-intel-14a-technology-at-its-20bn-terafab-project-in-austin/#comments)

[Facebook](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/#facebook) [Twitter](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/#twitter) [LinkedIn](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/#linkedin) [Reddit](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/#reddit) [Email](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/#email) [Share](https://www.addtoany.com/share#url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.datacenterdynamics.com%2Fen%2Fnews%2Felon-musk-says-tesla-will-use-intel-14a-technology-at-its-20bn-terafab-project-in-austin%2F&title=Elon%20Musk%20says%20Tesla%20will%20use%20Intel%2014A%20technology%20at%20its%20%2420bn%20TeraFab%20project%20in%20Austin%20-%20DCD)

Tesla CEO Elon Musk has said that the EV company is planning to use Intel’s 14A chip manufacturing process at its $20 billion ‘TeraFab’ project in Austin, Texas.

"We plan to use Intel's 14A process, which is state-of-the-art and in fact not yet totally complete," Musk said during Tesla’s Q1 2026 earnings call.

"By the time TeraFab scales up, 14A will be probably fairly mature or ready for prime time. 14A seems like the right move, and we have a great relationship with Intel, a lot of respect for the CEO, the CTO, and the new team there,” he added.

![Lip-Bu Tan and Elon Musk](https://media.datacenterdynamics.com/media/images/Lip-Bu_Tan_and_Elon_Musk.width-358.jpg)

– Intel

The news comes two weeks after the chipmaker officially [announced](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/intel-joins-elon-musks-20bn-terafab-project/) it had joined the TeraFab project via a post on the Musk-owned social media platform X, writing: “Our ability to design, fabricate, and package ultra-high-performance chips at scale will help accelerate TeraFab’s aim to produce 1 TW/year of compute to power future advances in AI and robotics.”

Musk’s commitment to Intel 14A marks a turnaround in fortunes for the chipmaker, which had previously mulled the cancellation of the technology as a result of financial concerns.

Following the publication of [Intel’s Q2 2025 earnings](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/intel-shutters-european-fab-construction-mulls-14a-cancellation-and-announces-more-job-cuts-amid-losses/) in July last year, the company’s CEO, Lip-Bu Tan, said that given its increased costs, Intel would only move forward with the technology if a “meaningful external customer to drive acceptable returns on our deployed capital” could be found.

“I do not subscribe to the belief that if you build it, they will come,” Tan further noted. “Under my leadership, we will build what customers need, when they need it, and earn their trust through consistent execution.”

Musk confirmed plans to build a semiconductor plant in Austin, Texas, in [March 2026](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/elon-musk-announces-terafab-20bn-factory-will-make-chips-for-spacex-orbital-data-centers-and-tesla-vehicles/), with the site set to be adjacent to Tesla’s headquarters and run as a joint venture between the automaker and SpaceX. Musk said the facility will produce chips for space data centers, advanced vehicles, and humanoid robots.

The idea was [first floated](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/elon-musk-says-tesla-will-probably-have-to-build-gigantic-chip-fab-and-might-do-something-with-intel/) by the world’s richest man at a Tesla annual shareholder meeting in November 2025. At the time, Musk said that if Tesla were to extrapolate the best-case scenario for chip production from its suppliers, it still wouldn’t be enough, which had led him to propose the Tesla ‘TeraFab’ – “it’s like giga but way bigger.”

On the most recent earnings call, Musk also revealed that in the near term, Tesla will build a $3bn R&D facility at the Gigafactory campus in Austin to support the production of a “few thousand wafers per month,” while long term, SpaceX will take responsibility for high-volume manufacturing at the facility.

“It is really intended to try out ideas… for improving the fundamental technology of how chips are made, some of the new physics we would like to test out. We also want to test out the ability to see if something is working in production \[environment\]. You need kind of like a few thousand wafer starts a month to make sure that a production process is sound,” Musk said.

"That is basically what we have figured out thus far: Tesla's doing the research fab, SpaceX's doing the initial part of the large-scale TeraFab, and then we've got to figure out the rest.”

In a presentation late last month at Seaholm Power Plant, the [tech mogul announced](https://www.statesman.com/business/article/terafab-austin-elon-musk-tesla-spacex-22091260.php) what he said would be “the largest chip manufacturing facility ever” as part of a [project dubbed Terafab](https://www.statesman.com/business/article/tesla-terafab-austin-construction-elon-musk-spacex-22096061.php). Now, it appears the site where he spoke was a clue about the role the redeveloped mixed-use complex will play in realizing the ambitious idea.

## xAI, Tesla, SpaceX linked to Seaholm lease

Reports from two commercial real estate firms suggest xAI and other Musk-led companies are leasing more than 112,000 square feet at Seaholm.

In its first quarter Austin [office report](https://assets.cushmanwakefield.com/-/media/cw/marketbeat-pdfs/2026/q1/us-reports/office/austin_americas_marketbeat_office_q12026.pdf?rev=c3b87448e1054c86bfcbd32c71b7b2ba&_gl=1*1x73ebe*_ga*MTMzOTAzMzg0LjE3NzY0Mzc5MzE.*_ga_LM51XKPGE6*czE3NzY0Mzc5MzEkbzEkZzEkdDE3NzY0Mzc5NzMkajYwJGwwJGgw*_ga_D68R2GB427*czE3NzY0Mzc5MzEkbzEkZzEkdDE3NzY0Mzc5NzMkajYwJGwwJGgw*_gcl_au*MTg2NTk3NTExNS4xNzc2NDM3OTM1*_ga_B63VJVKT85*czE3NzY0Mzc5MzUkbzEkZzEkdDE3NzY0Mzc5NzQkajIxJGwwJGgw), Cushman & Wakefield listed xAI’s as a key lease transaction. [CBRE](https://mktgdocs.cbre.com/2299/25c0341c-ed63-40eb-aa26-da0c36411924-574250362/Austin_Office_Figures_Q1_2026_.pdf) similarly listed a sublease of the space formerly occupied by Athena Health, tying it to a joint venture between Tesla Inc., SpaceX, xAI and Intel Corp.

Intel, a California semiconductor manufacturer, [recently announced its intention](https://www.statesman.com/business/article/intel-terafab-elon-musk-22193910.php) to join in the work on Terafab. The extent of its involvement is unclear. Publicly traded companies must submit a filing on significant financial news with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, but Intel has yet to do so on its involvement in Terafab.

## Terafab plans moving quickly in Austin

Construction is seen north of the Tesla Giga Texas factory in Austin on Wednesday, March 25, 2026. CEO Elon Musk said Tesla and SpaceX are planning the world’s largest chip manufacturing plant, called Terafab, but said this site would be used for a smaller facility focused on chip design.

Jay Janner/Austin American-Statesman

Plans for Terafab, which Musk said would start in Austin and include other sites that are still being surveyed, are moving quickly. As he announced plans to local officials last month, earthmovers already were at work on a site near Gigafactory Texas that Musk said later would be a small plant focused on advanced chip design.

The entire project — which he said could be more than 12 times the size of the massive Samsung Electronics chip plant in Taylor — would build chips for Tesla to use in its vehicles and [Optimus robots](https://www.statesman.com/business/technology/article/optimus-california-texas-production-gigafactory-21324292.php) and for SpaceX to use in the space data centers Musk has recently [begun touting.](https://www.statesman.com/business/article/spacex-xai-elon-musk-acquired-21329813.php)

Last week, he confirmed a [Bloomberg report](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-04-16/musk-asks-suppliers-to-move-at-light-speed-on-terafab-project?embedded-checkout=true) that his lieutenants have been asking chip industry suppliers for price quotes and delivery times for chipmaking equipment.

In a [separate post on X](https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2044844582777864676?s=46&t=jnykt_YuitlyjFPIhKKOrA), though, he acknowledged Terafab will be a demanding undertaking.

“Most people are under the impression that the idea/prototype is the hard part when it is 1% of the problem,” Musk said. “For example, the idea of going to the moon is trivial, actually doing it is the hard part!”

Once completed, Musk says the facility will support production of 160,000 semiconductor wafers a month.

## Hiring ramps up in Austin, elsewhere

Tesla has posted several engineering jobs tied to Terafab in Austin and others in Palo Alto, Calif. Tesla is also hiring in Taiwan, a leader in the semiconductor industry and home to TSMC, the company that produces most of the world’s most advanced chips.

April 23 (Reuters) - Tesla [(TSLA.O), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/TSLA.O) chief Elon Musk said on Wednesday the electric vehicle maker plans to use Intel's [(INTC.O), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/INTC.O) [next-generation 14A manufacturing process](https://www.reuters.com/business/autos-transportation/tesla-ceo-musk-says-company-plans-use-intels-14a-process-terafab-2026-04-22/) to make chips at its Terafab project, an advanced artificial-intelligence chip complex Musk has envisioned in Texas.

## WHAT IS THE TERAFAB PROJECT?

Musk's SpaceX, its xAI ​unit and Tesla will [build two advanced chip factories](https://www.reuters.com/business/autos-transportation/musk-says-spacex-tesla-build-advanced-chip-factories-austin-2026-03-22/) at a sprawling facility in Austin, one to be used in ‌Tesla vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots, and another designed for AI data centers in space.

"We either build the Terafab or we don't have the chips," Musk had said during a presentation in Austin in March, adding that current global chip production would meet only a small fraction of his companies' future needs.

Musk ​said he was grateful to existing chip suppliers, naming Samsung [(005930.KS), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/005930.KS), TSMC [(2330.TW), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/2330.TW) and Micron [(MU.O), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/MU.O), but said demand from his companies would ​eventually exceed total global chip output.

He did not give a timeline for the project and has a track ⁠record of announcing highly ambitious projects, though several have faced delays or fallen away.

Intel announced it would [join the project](https://www.reuters.com/business/autos-transportation/intel-join-musks-terafab-mega-ai-chip-project-2026-04-07/) in April, bringing ​established chip manufacturing expertise to the venture.

Advertisement · Scroll to continue

## LOCATION AND SCALE

Musk has said the Terafab will handle each step of chip production, including the design.

On ​Tesla's earnings call on Wednesday, Musk said that the details of the Terafab deployment are still being worked out.

In the near term, Tesla will be building the research fab on its Giga Texas campus in the Austin area. The initiative is expected to cost about $3 billion and "capable of maybe a few thousand ​wafers per month, but it's really intended to try out ideas," Musk said.

"What we figured out thus far is Tesla doing the ​research fab, SpaceX doing the initial part of the large-scale Terafab. And then we got to figure out the rest," he said.

Terafab will eventually produce ‌one terawatt ⁠of computing capacity a year, compared with about half a terawatt currently generated across the United States, Musk had said in March.

Building enough chip capacity to power one terawatt of annual compute would cost between $5 trillion and $13 trillion in capital expenditure, according to Bernstein estimates.

## TECHNOLOGY

Tesla plans to use Intel's 14A manufacturing process to make chips at the Terafab project. The contract would mark Intel's first major customer for the ​technology, a breakthrough for the chipmaker ​which has struggled to stand ⁠up its contract manufacturing business essential for taking on top rival TSMC.

Musk said that by the time Terafab scales up, Intel's 14A manufacturing process "will be probably fairly mature or ready for prime time" and "seems ​like the right move."

Musk's staff have [reached out](https://www.reuters.com/business/autos-transportation/musks-staff-reaches-out-suppliers-terafab-project-bloomberg-news-reports-2026-04-16/) to chip industry suppliers, including Applied Materials [(AMAT.O), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/AMAT.O), Tokyo Electron [(8035.T), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/8035.T) ​and Lam Research [(LRCX.O), opens new tab](https://www.reuters.com/markets/companies/LRCX.O), ⁠and Samsung for the Terafab project, according to Bloomberg.

Staff have sought price quotes and delivery times for an array of chipmaking gear, Bloomberg reported last week, adding that in the past few weeks, they have contacted makers of photomasks, substrates, etchers, depositors, cleaning devices, testers and other tools.

Reuters ⁠reported that [SpaceX ​is planning to make its own graphics processing units](https://www.reuters.com/business/autos-transportation/spacex-targets-in-house-gpus-it-warns-investors-chip-supply-costs-2026-04-23/), or GPUs, the chips at ​the heart of training AI models.

## THE "UNKNOWNS"

Though Musk has said Terafab would target chips for cars, humanoid robots and space-based data centers, many details are unknown, such as:

- Who will ​pay for pricey chipmaking equipment

- Who will operate the factory

- When it will come online

## **Elon Musk [has picked](https://money.usnews.com/investing/news/articles/2026-04-22/tesla-ceo-musk-says-company-plans-to-use-intels-14a-process-for-terafab) Intel’s unproven next-generation node to feed chips into his Austin Terafab complex, handing the struggling foundry its first real outside customer and a lifeline Lip Bu Tan said Intel needed to survive in manufacturing.**

![Close up of hand holding Intel® Core™ Ultra Series 3 - blur outside](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns=%22http://www.w3.org/2000/svg%22%20viewBox=%220%200%201920%201280%22%3E%3C/svg%3E)Close up of hand holding Intel® Core™ Ultra Series 3 – blur outside

### **Key Takeaways:**

- Tesla becomes Intel’s first announced external customer for its 14A node, which will feed chips into Musk’s Austin Terafab project.
- Intel CEO Lip Bu Tan had previously warned that Intel would walk away from chip manufacturing entirely without an outside customer on 14A.
- Musk’s Terafab is targeting one terawatt of annual compute — roughly double current U.S. output — at an estimated cost of $5 trillion to $13 trillion, per Bernstein.

Elon Musk confirmed on Wednesday that Tesla will lean on Intel’s forthcoming 14A manufacturing process to build chips inside Terafab, the sprawling AI chip complex he wants to erect in Austin. The contract makes Tesla the first high-profile outside name attached to a node that Intel has been quietly pitching for months, and it hands the chipmaker something it desperately needed: proof that someone beyond Intel itself is willing to bet on its factories.

The stakes for Intel are hard to overstate. CEO Lip Bu Tan has said openly that the company would abandon contract manufacturing altogether if it could not land an external buyer for 14A — a blunt admission that the foundry business, long pitched as Intel’s comeback vehicle against TSMC, was running out of runway. Intel shares climbed 3.6% in extended trading on the news. The company declined to comment on Musk’s statement.

Intel had signaled earlier that conversations with major customers were underway, but no name had emerged publicly. Tesla fills that blank. Earlier this month Intel joined Terafab alongside SpaceX and Tesla, positioning itself to supply the processors Musk says will eventually power his humanoid robots, vehicle fleets, and orbital data centers.

## The Terafab Math

Terafab is not a modest project. Musk said in March that SpaceX and Tesla would build two advanced chip factories on the site — one dedicated to vehicles and robots, another purpose-built for space-based data centers. Most operational questions remain unanswered: who pays for the chipmaking equipment, who runs the fab day-to-day, and when any of it actually comes online. What Musk has committed to publicly is an annual output target of one terawatt of computing capacity, against roughly half a terawatt currently produced across the entire United States.

Bernstein analysts put the capital cost of building chip capacity on that scale at somewhere between $5 trillion and $13 trillion. For context, the entire U.S. semiconductor industry does not spend anything close to that figure in a decade.

Tesla also lifted its own capital spending plans sharply on Wednesday, with Musk framing the higher outlay as necessary fuel for new revenue streams. Investors were lukewarm, nudging Tesla shares slightly lower in after-hours trading. Musk has sold shareholders on sweeping visions before — ubiquitous humanoid robots, data centers orbiting Earth — and has collected a reputation for loose schedules and deadlines that slip past without fanfare.

## Why Musk Picked 14A

> “Given that by the time Terafab scales up, 14A will be probably fairly mature or ready for prime time. 14A seems like the right move, and we have a great relationship with Intel,” commented Elon Musk.

Industry analysts read the deal as more consequential than the Terafab headline suggests, precisely because the Terafab timeline is so uncertain. Ben Bajarin, who heads the technology consultancy Creative Strategies, said Intel’s 14A could “turn out to be a bigger deal for Intel than folks thought.” He argued that early design partners at the leading edge play an outsized role in working out the kinks of a new process.

> ## Real Volumes

Jay Goldberg of Seaport Research Partners landed on a similar conclusion from a different direction. The unknowns around Terafab, he said, matter less than the fact of a customer signature itself. Musk’s projections about how many chips Tesla’s robots might one day demand may or may not pan out — but producing silicon for Tesla’s existing product lines alone would still be a meaningful commercial win for Intel.

> “Having a customer is more important than the timing. It’s not equivalent to Apple or Nvidia. But it’s a real customer. It can be real volumes,” said Jay Goldberg.
>
> That is the test Intel now faces. The 14A node has a patron willing to publicly vouch for it, which is more than the chipmaker could claim a month ago. Whether Terafab delivers on its terawatt ambition is almost a separate question — because even a fraction of Musk’s projected volumes would put Intel’s foundry business back on the map.

# Intel lands Tesla as first major customer for 14A chip technology

Fargo, ND, USA / The Mighty 790 KFGO \| KFGO

[Thomson Reuters](mailto:)

Apr 22, 2026 \| 5:29 PM

![](https://storage.googleapis.com/media.mwcradio.com/mimesis/2026-04/22/2026-04-22T222942Z_1_LYNXMPEM3L1GN_RTROPTP_3_XCORP-ADVERTISING-LAWSUIT.JPG)

By Zaheer Kachwala and Stephen Nellis

April 22 (Reuters) – Tesla CEO Elon Musk said on Wednesday the EV maker plans to use Intel’s next-generation 14A manufacturing process to make chips at its Terafab project, an advanced AI chip complex Musk has envisioned in Austin.

The contract would mark Intel’s first major customer for ​the technology, a breakthrough for the chipmaker which has struggled to stand up its contract manufacturing ‌business essential for taking on top rival TSMC. Intel CEO Lip Bu Tan has said that the company would exit the chip manufacturing business altogether if it failed to secure an external customer.

Intel has previously said it was in discussions with large customers about 14A, but has not yet disclosed a major external customer. It declined to comment on Musk’s remarks.

The chipmaker’s shares rose 3.6% in extended trading.

Intel joined Musk’s ‌Terafab ​AI chip complex earlier this month with SpaceX and Tesla to make processors ⁠to fuel the billionaire’s robotics and data ⁠center ambitions. Tesla on Wednesday sharply boosted its capital investment plans, with Musk saying the outlay was necessary to fuel future revenue streams.

The carmaker’s investors were less than impressed, pushing its stock down slightly after hours. Musk, who has wooed investors with his promises to build ubiquitous humanoid robots and data centers in space, has ​also drawn criticism for his loose timelines and often-missed deadlines.

The Terafab, too, would be a massive undertaking. Musk said in March his space startup SpaceX and Tesla would build two advanced chip factories at this sprawling facility, one to ⁠power cars and humanoid robots, and another designed for the space ⁠data centers.

Many details of the Terafab project – such as who will pay for pricey chipmaking ​equipment, who will operate the factory and when it will come online – remain unknown. Musk has said, though, that Terafab ​will eventually produce one terawatt of computing capacity a year, compared with about half a terawatt ‌currently generated across the United States.

Building enough chip capacity to power one terawatt of annual compute would cost between $5 trillion and $13 trillion in capital expenditure, according to Bernstein estimates.

REAL VOLUMES

For Intel shareholders, though, this is good news.

“Given that by the time Terafab scales up, 14A will be probably fairly mature or ready for prime time,” Musk said. “14A seems like the right ⁠move, and we have a great relationship with Intel,” he said.

Ben Bajarin, head of technology consultancy Creative Strategies, said that Intel’s 14A technology could “turn out to be a bigger deal for Intel than folks thought.”

“It’s important to have multiple partners as ⁠early design partners to help clean the ‌pipe and work through needed learnings at the leading edge. They will definitely have ⁠scale, so a great first non-Intel customer,” Bajarin said.

Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay ​Goldberg said Musk’s ‌vote of confidence in Intel’s technology outweighed the unknowns about the Terafab project.

“Having ​a customer is ⁠more important than the timing,” he said.

Goldberg said that Musk’s lofty estimates of how many chips its robots could one day require may or may not materialize, but even making chips for Tesla’s existing businesses would be a significant win for Intel.

“It’s not equivalent to Apple or Nvidia” in terms of chip volumes, Goldberg said. “But it’s a real customer. It can be real volumes.”

(Reporting by Zaheer Kachwala and Aditya Soni in Bengaluru and Stephen Nellis in Morgan Hill, California; Editing by Deepa Babington, ​Sayantani Ghosh and Kim Coghill)
